es.q: Discuss the distinguishing features of autosomal dominant inheritance patterns in terms of family history, molecular theme, and typical age of onset.
es.m:
**Key points:**
- Disease appears in every generation with no skipping.
- Affected parent has a 50% chance of passing the abnormal allele to each child.
- Both sexes are equally affected.
- Molecular theme involves structural proteins (e.g., fibrillin‑1 in Marfan syndrome).
- Onset is often in adulthood.

exam: A 28‑year‑old man presents with tendon xanthomas and LDL‑C 250 mg/dL; his father died of MI at 45 – what is the most likely inheritance and next step? — AD familial hypercholesterolaemia; obtain lipid profile of first‑degree relatives and start statin therapy.

A child has macrocytic anaemia, reticulocytopenia and a father with mild anaemia; bone marrow shows reduced erythroid precursors – which inheritance pattern and disease? — AD Diamond‑Blackfan anaemia; confirm with peripheral smear and consider steroids.
A 45‑year‑old woman with iron overload has normal ferritin but transferrin saturation 65 % – what does this indicate? — Early hereditary haemochromatosis (AD); start phlebotomy and screen relatives.

During a ward round you note a patient with hereditary elliptocytosis; what key family history feature supports AD inheritance? — Presence of the trait in at least two successive generations on both maternal and paternal sides.

A patient from a malaria‑endemic area has unexplained anaemia; smear shows elliptocytes – how do you differentiate hereditary from acquired causes? — Look for family history, chronic liver disease, or drug exposure; hereditary persists despite treating malaria.

In a low‑resource clinic you cannot measure transferrin saturation; what clinical clues suggest haemochromatosis? — Skin hyperpigmentation, hepatomegaly, early arthropathy, and a positive family history of iron‑related disease.

Why are statins preferred over fibrates in familial hypercholesterolaemia in East African settings? — Statins directly lower LDL‑C, the primary driver of premature atherosclerosis; fibrates mainly lower triglycerides and may increase liver enzymes.
A newborn of a mother with AD Alport syndrome shows haematuria – what counseling is needed? — Explain 50 % transmission risk, need for renal monitoring, and that disease severity can vary.
ai.title: Autosomal Dominant Inheritance
ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Autosomal dominant inheritance means a single mutant allele can cause disease, often with variable expression. Recognising patterns helps clinicians anticipate family risk and guide testing in low‑resource settings.

b: Vertical transmission across generations
Often variable penetrance and expressivity
New (de novo) mutations account for ~30 % of cases
sections.p: In autosomal dominant (AD) disorders the disease‑causing gene is on a non‑sex chromosome and one mutated copy is enough to produce the phenotype. Each child of an affected parent has a 50 % chance of inheriting the mutation.

b: Dominant‑negative: mutant protein blocks normal protein (e.g., collagen VII in dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa)
Haploinsufficiency: 50 % protein insufficient for normal function (e.g., TBX1 in DiGeorge syndrome)
sections.p: A normal allele produces functional protein; the mutant allele either produces a defective protein that interferes with the normal one (dominant‑negative) or reduces overall protein dosage (haploinsufficiency).

b: No imprinting effect in classic AD traits
Mosaicism may modify severity
sections.p: Gene expression is controlled by promoters, enhancers and epigenetic marks. In AD disease the mutant allele is usually expressed at the same level as the wild‑type allele, so the abnormal protein is present in every cell.

b: Ribosomopathies: RP gene mutations → defective erythropoiesis (AD in ~70 % of cases)
Hereditary haemochromatosis: HFE C282Y heterozygosity → iron overload
Familial hypercholesterolaemia: LDLR or APOB mutation → premature atherosclerosis
sections.p: Pathogenic variants disrupt protein structure or quantity, leading to organ‑specific disease. In low‑resource settings, common AD disorders include hereditary haemochromatosis, familial hypercholesterolaemia, and certain ribosomopathies such as Diamond‑Blackfan anaemia.

b: Take a three‑generation pedigree; look for vertical transmission
Screen first‑degree relatives early (e.g., lipid profile for FH)
Consider de novo mutation if no family history but classic phenotype
sections.p: Identifying an AD pattern guides counselling, screening of relatives, and selection of appropriate investigations, even when sophisticated tests are unavailable.

t.b: Does the family show vertical transmission? → Confirms AD pattern, prompts targeted testing
Are there abnormal cells (e.g., elliptocytes, macrocytes)? → Suggests ribosomopathy or hereditary elliptocytosis
Is iron overload present? → Supports hereditary haemochromatosis; if unavailable, use liver function tests and clinical signs
Is LDL‑C markedly elevated? → Indicates familial hypercholesterolaemia; if lab unavailable, assess tendon xanthomas clinically
Which gene is mutated? → Confirms diagnosis, informs prognosis; if not available, rely on phenotype and family history

b: Hereditary haemochromatosis: regular phlebotomy; avoid iron supplements
Familial hypercholesterolaemia: high‑intensity statin (if available) or diet + plant sterols; avoid fibrates in liver disease
Diamond‑Blackfan anaemia: transfusion support; consider corticosteroids if feasible
sections.p: Treat the disease manifestation, then address the genetic risk. In low‑resource hospitals, emphasis is on simple, evidence‑based interventions.

b: Autosomal recessive disorders – require two mutant alleles, often no vertical transmission
X‑linked dominant – affects males more severely and shows sex‑linked pattern
Normal ferritin does not exclude early haemochromatosis; rely on transferrin saturation
Mild LDL‑C rise may be missed in fasting‑noncompliant patients; look for physical signs
Always draw a three‑generation pedigree for suspected AD disease
Remember that variable penetrance can produce an apparently unaffected parent

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden cardiac death in a young relative with familial hypercholesterolaemia
Severe iron overload causing liver failure or cardiomyopathy
